## editor/clipboard

The clipboard as the editor's menu reaches it, beside the keys:
the selection as markdown, markdown pasted as what it stands for, and the
clipboard read for a Paste chosen from the menu.

Cut, Copy and the keys' Paste are the editor's own: the view writes and
reads the clipboard in its copy and paste events, with the document's
formatting as HTML. A paste chosen from a menu has no paste event, so the
clipboard is read instead, which a browser may ask the writer to allow.

## editor/commentDraft

The passage a new comment is being written on, while it is
written somewhere else: in the Comments tab, beside the text.

The passage has no mark yet, since the comment may never be made, but it
has to follow the text as a mark would while the writer looks away to
write: typing before it moves it, and deleting it takes the draft with it.
So it is a range in the editor's state, mapped through every transaction,
and tinted in the text as an open field's passage is.

Returns **Plugin<([DraftRange][24] | null)>**&#x20;

## editor/comments

A comment on a passage: its place in the text, and its thread
on the document's row.

A writer highlights a run of text and says something about it; the model
reads it, answers, and resolves it. The passage has to survive every edit
around it and every round trip through the file format, so its place is in
the text itself: a mark in the editor and, in the markdown, CriticMarkup
that holds only an id:

    We had a {==cold and narrow==}{>>c7k2m1<<} attic.

What was said, by whom, and the replies are the thread, kept on the
document's row as `comments`, by that id (see `CommentThread`). A thread is
placed while its id is in the text; an open one whose id is not is stale,
its passage deleted, and undoing the delete places it again.

Comments may overlap. In the editor several comment marks can sit on the
same text. In the markup one comment nests inside another, and where two
only partly overlap, one of them is written in pieces, each with its id, as
one over two paragraphs is:

    We had a {==cold and {==narrow==}{>>c2<<}==}{>>c1<<}{== attic==}{>>c2<<}.

A close ends the innermost comment still open. Text without overlaps reads
as it always did.

Until 16 Oct 2026 what was said was in the markup too, as
`{>>c7k2m1: reword this<<}`, with each break written `<br>`. That form is
still read: `liftThreads` moves what it says onto a thread, which is how a
document from before is brought forward.

Everything here is pure: the pattern, the helpers over a string and over
threads, and the markdown-it rules the parser runs. The mark spec is in
`schema.js` and the serializer rule in `markdown.js`, both built on what is
here.

## Threads

Type: Record<[string][1055], CommentThread>

## commentMarkupPlugin

The markdown-it rules that read the markup: one that opens a comment at
`{==` when its close is ahead, past any comment inside it, and one that
closes the innermost comment open at `==}{>>…<<}`. The parser maps
`comment_open` and `comment_close` to the mark, both with the id, so that
a close ends only its own comment (see `markdown.js`).

A rule scanning past text without reading it, as a link does to find the
end of its text, runs the rules silently, and each has to move past what
it matched: to it a comment is one thing, so a `]` in what was said does
not end the link. A close another rule swallows — a code span running
over it — leaves its open with nothing to end it, and that open is put
back as the text it was, so a comment never runs on past its paragraph.

How many comments are open is counted for each parse of a run of text,
not in the parser's `env`, which a picture's alt text, read in a parse of
its own, shares with the passage around it.

### Parameters

- `md` &#x20;

## editor/comparison

A version of a document against its text now, as one
document for the Versions dialog to show: the version as the editor would
show it, with what a restore would take out of the text now marked as
deletions, and what it would bring back as insertions, both under an id of
the comparison's own.

The change is laid out as a suggested one is (`layOut` in
`suggestions.js`): block by block, then word by word in the blocks it
changed, a block with no words to mark taken out or brought back whole. It
is laid out from the version to the text now, so that what both have is
the version's, its comments and pending suggestions with it, and what the
version alone has that a pending suggestion is on is shown as that
suggestion. Then it is turned round to say what a restore does, and in
each change what goes comes first.

Nothing here is written: no markup can hold the comparison's id, and what
is copied from it is the version's own text (`versionBetween`).

## editor/format

What the formatting buttons over a selection offer: the marks
on the selected text, the style of the blocks it is in, and whether they
are quoted or listed, with the commands that change each.

A mark is toggled as its key toggles it: taken off where any of the
selection has it, put on otherwise. A style is the kind of text block —
normal text, a heading, a code block — and one replaces another. Quotes and
lists hold blocks rather than being them, so each is on or off around the
style: off lifts the selected blocks out of the nearest one, and a list of
the other kind becomes this kind. There is no underline, which markdown
cannot write (see `editor/schema`).

## editor/formulas

Formulas in the editor: TeX typeset by KaTeX where it stands,
and opened as it is written to be changed. Design:
`.llm/math_design.md`.

A formula is a leaf holding its TeX (`editor/schema.js`). Its node view
draws it typeset, or as written while KaTeX is on its way, or in KaTeX's
error colour, KaTeX's message on hover, when KaTeX can't read it.

Clicked, or arrowed onto, it opens: a field in its place holding it as it
is written, delimiters and all, the caret just inside the end it was come
at from, and the formula typeset under it as it is typed. Arrowing out past
either end closes it, as do Escape, Enter in a sentence's formula and
Mod-Enter in one of its own (where Enter is a new line of TeX), and a click
elsewhere. What the field holds is read back as markdown as it closes, one
change for Mod-Z to take back: still one formula, it is that formula with
its new TeX; a dollar taken out, it is text again; two written, they are
two; nothing, and it is gone. A formula an undo puts back is selected, not
opened; Enter opens it.

Typed, `$…$` becomes a formula when the character after its closing dollar
is typed, unless that is a digit (so "$5–$10" stays two prices), or on
Enter; `$$…$$` in a sentence too. `$$` at the start of an empty paragraph
is a formula of its own, opened. Insert › Formula and Mod-Shift-E put one
in at the caret, take the selection's words as its TeX, or in an empty
paragraph make one of its own.

## Side

Type: (`"start"` | `"end"`)

## editor

The document model and the editor's state: a closed schema,
the markdown that is its file format, and the `EditorState` a document
becomes while it is open.

- **schema** - The nodes and marks a document can hold
- **markdown** - `parseMarkdown` and `serializeMarkdown`, the two directions
  of the file format; `settleMarkdown` for text from outside; `appendBlocks`
  for joining markdown to markdown
- **comments** - A comment on a passage: the markup, the helpers, the parser rules, and
  the entries a list shows
- **suggestions** - A suggested change: its markup and parser rules, a change
  laid out as one suggestion for each change in it, folded into the model's
  own where it touches them, where each is, and one accepted or rejected
- **suggestionText** - The same in markdown: whether a text holds any, the
  text as one reader sees it, and a model's text with its markup read as meant
- **comparison** - A version against the text now, laid out as a suggestion
  is, for the Versions dialog to show: what a restore would take out and
  bring back, and the version's own text to copy out of it
- **streaming** - Text the model is still writing into an append, drawn at
  the end of the document as it arrives by a widget, and written only when
  the call runs
- **commentDraft** - The passage a new comment is being written on in the
  Comments tab: a range in the state, mapped through every change and tinted
- **state** - `createEditorState`, the keys and typed shortcuts, and the
  `replaceContent` and `appendContent` transactions an outside writer asks for
- **search** - Find and replace: the matches as a plugin's state, drawn as
  decorations, and the commands that move between and replace them
- **spelling** - What the spelling checker found, drawn under the text, and
  the commands its menu runs; see `spelling/`
- **clipboard** - The selection as markdown, markdown pasted as what it
  stands for, and the clipboard read for a Paste from the editor's menu
- **insert** - A table, a horizontal rule or a code block put in from the
  editor's menu, where it is otherwise only typed
- **plainSearch** - The same for a plain document, in the CodeMirror view it
  is shown in; loaded with that view, so not exported here
- **projectSearch** - Find across a project: every document with the query,
  each match on its line, counted as the document's own find counts them
- **plainMacros** - A card's `{{char}}`, `{{user}}` and the rest picked out
  in that view; loaded with it too
- **size** - `laysOut`, whether a document is short enough for the editor
  to lay out, which decides how a long import comes in
- **tables** - A table made by typing its header row, the keys that move
  through one, rows and columns inserted from the menu, column alignment,
  and pasting into a cell
- **links** - Making, changing, removing and opening links: the commands,
  and a view plugin for Mod-K, Mod-click and a pasted link
- **pictures** - Pictures in the text: a node view that draws one from
  what the editor component says its path is, a picture from the web as a
  placeholder that fetches nothing, figures, and the object URLs the bytes
  are shown on
- **formulas** - TeX typeset where it stands, opened as it is written in a
  field in its place, typed as `$x^2$` or `$$`, and put in from the menu
- **format** - What the formatting buttons over a selection offer: its
  marks, its blocks' style, quoted or listed, and the commands that change
  them
- **marks** - `markAround`, the run of a mark around a position, for the
  link or the comment the caret is in
- **shortcuts** - The keys and typed shortcuts as the writer is shown them,
  on Mod-/, spelled for their keyboard

`Document.content` is markdown. While a document is open — in a tab, with
or without a view over it — its `EditorState` is the truth and the store's
copy is a projection of it, serialized on a debounce (see
`composables/useEditor`); closed, the store's markdown is the truth. A
plain document (`Document.plain`) never becomes an `EditorState`: its text
is the truth while open and is stored as typed, so a prompt keeps whatever
the schema could not hold, and an import too long to lay out comes in as
one. The AI tools read and write it as it is; the v13 migration produced
it from the HTML that came before. Design: `.llm/markdown_library_design.md`.

### Examples

```javascript
import { parseMarkdown, serializeMarkdown } from '@/editor/markdown'
const doc = parseMarkdown('# Chapter One\n\nIt was a dark night.')
serializeMarkdown(doc) // '# Chapter One\n\nIt was a dark night.'
```

## editor/insert

Blocks put in from the editor's menu, for what is otherwise only
typed: a table (`| a | b |` and Enter), a horizontal rule (`---`) and a code
block (three backticks).

A block takes the place of an empty paragraph the caret is in. Otherwise it
goes after the block the caret is in, or as far out as it can go from
there: after a table, not in its cell. The caret goes where the writing
goes on: a table's first cell, a code block, or a paragraph after a rule.

## editor/linkPicker

`[[` and a name, for a link to another document.

Typing `[[` in a paragraph opens a list of the project's documents under
the caret, which narrows as a name is typed after it, and a `#` goes on to
a document's headings (`[[Cast list#The crew`, or `[[#The crew` for this

typed again. Not in code, where `[[` is code.

The list is the editor component's to show; this says where it is and

## editor/links

Links in a document: making one, changing or removing it, and
opening it, the way Google Docs does.

Mod-K links the selection, or changes the link the caret is in; with
nothing selected it puts in a new link, words and all. A click in a link
puts the caret there like a click anywhere, and the editor shows the link
beside it (see `LinkPopover.vue`); Mod-click opens it. A link pasted over a
selection links the selection, and one pasted on its own goes in as a link.

The commands are the state's; the keys, the clicks and the paste are a view
plugin's, since what they do next — show a field, open a page — is the
editor component's to do. So is how a link is carried from one document to
another, which `mapHrefs` changes in a copied or pasted slice.

## editor/markdown

Markdown as the document's file format: what the store holds,
what the model reads and writes, and what a file on disk will be.

Built on `prosemirror-markdown`, the reference implementation, with the
parser and serializer configured against our schema rather than inherited.
The parser is markdown-it's `default` preset — CommonMark plus GFM
strikethrough and tables — with raw HTML off, so a tag in a document is
text. A picture's alt text is its words as plain text, marks and all
dropped, as markdown-it writes it in HTML.

A table is written the plainest way GFM reads: a pipe at each end of every
row, one space inside each, and no padding to line the columns up, so that
an edit to one cell is an edit to one line. A pipe in a cell is escaped,
inside code as well, since the row is cut at its pipes before anything else
is read. markdown-it keeps as many cells in a row as the header has and
drops the rest, so a table with a row longer than its header is read as the
text it was written as, whole: words are not lost to a save.

A lone newline is a hard break, in both directions. A writer who ended a line
meant it to end there, and CommonMark's soft wrap is not a reading anyone
here expects. The serializer writes a hard break as a bare newline; when
several run together, the ones after the first are written backslash-newline,
which markdown-it reads as a hard break wherever it stands, so a run of
breaks comes back as the same run rather than as a blank line that would
split the paragraph.

Text is escaped where the reference would leave it to come back as
something else: an entity as its character, an address in angle brackets as
a link, `1)` at the start of a line as a list, a `#` ending a heading as
its closing. A space between words is bold, italic or struck only where
the words on both sides of it are: one left in bold after bold italic
would sit between the delimiters, and markdown would read them as text.

A formula is read before markdown's escapes, by the delimiters the chat
reads (`utils/tex.js`), and its TeX written as it is: `$…$` in a sentence,
or `\(…\)` where dollars can't hold it, and `$$`, its TeX and `$$` on lines
of their own. `\[…\]` is no formula here, since a bracket in the text is
written `\[`. A dollar in the
text is written `\$` only where it would otherwise open a formula, so a
price stays as it is: each is written as a mark first, and once the whole
is written, each mark, the last first, is a dollar or an escaped one by
what is written after it.

Two properties are pinned by tests: `parse(serialize(doc))` is `doc` for
every node and mark, and `serialize(parse(md))` is a fixed point after one
pass, which is what matters once files are edited outside the app.

## LinearSerializer

**Extends MarkdownSerializer**

The reference serializer, writing in time linear in the document's length.

Its state asks whether its output ends a line before nearly every block, and
a string grown a piece at a time is copied whole to be read. In a long
document that copy is the whole document, made again for every block: 20
seconds for a 1.5 MB rulebook in Chromium, 40 in WebKit, every time it was
saved, and as long for a list of 20,000 items. Here the state holds only the
end of its output, and what comes before is moved out as it is written, so
it answers the same, at once, at any depth.

### serialize

The document written, its text's dollars each a mark until what is
written after them says whether they are escaped. A mark is a character
the document has none of: should the first be in it already, the next is
tried, and with none left every dollar is escaped.

## editor/pictures

Pictures in the editor: each drawn by a node view, a
paragraph that is only a picture shown as a figure, a picture opened at its
own size on Mod-click or a double click, and pictures pasted, dropped or
inserted made the document's own.

What a picture's path is the editor component's to say (`describe`): one
of the document's own, a file document, an address on the web, or nothing
there. The view draws what it is told. A picture whose size is known keeps
its room while its bytes are read, so the text below stays where it is.
One from the web is never fetched: it is a placeholder naming its host,
since a picture that loads by itself sends its address the moment it is
on screen, and a model can be led to write one with the writer's words in
it. The page's Content-Security-Policy refuses it anyway.

Bytes are shown on object URLs, one for each picture however many nodes
show it, and let go of a little after the last node goes, so that an undo
or a redraw does not read them again.

A picture comes in as a file: pasted (a screenshot), dropped from the
desktop, or chosen from the menu (`insertPictures`). Pasted HTML that
carries a picture in an `img`'s source (`data:`) brings it in the same way.
Making it the document's own, and saying its path, is the editor
component's (`take`), and so is copying one pasted from another document
(`adopt`).

- `missing` - Nothing there that is a picture; `label` says what was asked for

## editor/plainSearch

Find and replace in a plain document, as `search` does it in a
laid-out one, for the CodeMirror view a plain document is shown in.

The matches are a state field, so they follow the text as it changes, and
they are drawn as decorations, in the classes `search` draws with. Case
and whole words count as they do there, and so does a replacement taking
the capitals of what it replaces. Moving to a match selects it, which is where the caret is
when the find is closed, and where a replace or the next search starts
from. Each command takes the view, as CodeMirror's own do, and says whether
there was anything to do; `reveal` then brings the match into sight.

Loaded with the plain view rather than from `editor/index`, so that
CodeMirror is not in the app until a plain document is opened.

## editor/projectSearch

Find across a project: every document that has what the
writer looks for, with the line each match is on, found as the document's
own find would find it.

A document laid out is found in as the editor finds (`search`): in the
text its markdown makes, block by block, so "the long road" finds "the
**long** road", and nothing is found in a link's address or a comment's
id. A plain document, and a file's text, are found in as their field finds
(`plainSearch`): in the text as it is. Either way the matches are counted
in the order that find comes to them, so the third here is the third
there, and going to it is asking the document's view for its third match.

Making the text of a laid-out document means reading its markdown, which
is the cost of a search. So a document is read only when its markdown has
every word of the query in it, which is a document that might match; and
what was read is kept, by document, for as long as its markdown is the
same, so the next letter typed reads nothing again. A document open in the
editor is found in as it stands there.

## editor/schema

The document schema: exactly the nodes and marks that have a
markdown form, and nothing else.

The markdown serializer is the file format, so the schema decides what a
document can hold. A node without a markdown representation would round-trip
to nothing, silently — underline is the concrete example — which is why the
set is declared here, one spec at a time, and pinned by a test rather than
inherited from whatever a starter kit ships with this year.

The specs are `prosemirror-schema-basic`'s and `prosemirror-schema-list`'s,
plus strikethrough, a code block that keeps its language, and GFM's table. Their `parseDOM` rules are what the v13 migration read the
old HTML through, so `<b>`, `<i>`, and `<s>` are covered as well as the tags
the editor writes.

A table is what GFM can write: a grid of one-line cells, the first row its
header, each column aligned or not. So a cell holds text and formulas and
nothing else — no break, which would end the row — and the header is the
first row because it is first: there is one kind of cell, and no way to put
a header row anywhere markdown could not. The cells carry `colspan` and
`rowspan` only because `prosemirror-tables` reads them; nothing sets them,
and they are always 1.

A picture is markdown's image, inline, since markdown has no picture as a
block. Its `src` is a path: to one of the document's own pictures, to a file
document, or an address on the web, which is never fetched (see
`editor/pictures.js`). Pasted HTML keeps an `img` whose source is one of
those, or the picture itself (`data:image/…`), which the paste makes one
of the document's own; one held by the page it came from (`blob:`) or on
the disk it came from (`file:`) is no picture to keep.

A formula is TeX between dollars (`utils/tex.js`): `formula` in a sentence,
`formula_block` on lines of its own. Each is a leaf holding its TeX, so
whatever reads the document's words reads a formula as one of them. Pasted
HTML keeps the editor's own element for one, KaTeX's, and MathML that
carries its TeX.

## comment

A comment's place: its id, carried on the passage it is about so that it
follows the text through every edit. What was said is the comment's
thread, on the document's row. Not inclusive, so typing at the edge of a
commented passage is outside it. It excludes nothing, itself included, so
comments with other ids can be on the same text: overlapping comments are
several marks. The markdown form is in `comments.js`.

## suggested

A suggested change's two halves: what it would put in, and what it would
take out, each carrying the suggestion's id. Until the writer accepts or
rejects it, the text holds both. On words, or on a whole block that has
none to carry it: a code block, a rule, a table, an empty block. Neither is
inclusive, so typing at the edge of one is outside it, and each excludes
the other and itself: a word is in one suggestion, one way. The markdown
form is in `suggestions.js`.

## editor/search

Find and replace in a document: what matches, which match is the
one the writer is on, and the transactions that move between the matches and
replace them.

The matches are a plugin's state, so they live with the document they were
found in and follow its text as it changes, and they are drawn as
decorations: nothing is written into the document to show them. A match is
within one textblock, a paragraph or a heading or a code block, whatever
marks it runs across: "the long road" finds "the **long** road". Case does
not count unless asked to, and a query is found inside longer words unless
asked for whole words only: "he" in "The" is how Replace all writes "Tshe".
With case not counting, a replacement typed in lower case takes the
capitals of what it replaces, so "he" for "she" makes "He" "She".

Moving to a match selects it, which is where the caret is when the find is
closed, and where a replace or the next search starts from. The commands
leave scrolling to the view, which knows how much of the page there is to
show it in.

## editor/size

How long a document the editor lays out.

The editor puts the whole of a document in the page, and every key typed in
it costs in proportion to how much is there: its paragraphs, list items and
table cells, not its characters. A novel kept in one document is a few
thousand paragraphs and types as fast as a page. A long reference with its
tables runs to tens of thousands, and the keys lag behind the writer. A
document past the limit comes in from outside as plain text, which is shown
a screen at a time whatever its length, and can be laid out from its menu.

## LAYOUT_LIMIT

How many nodes a document can have and still come in laid out.

Type: [number][1060]

## editor/spelling

Spelling and grammar in the editor: what the checker found,
drawn under the text, and the commands the menu on a flagged word runs.

The plugin's state is what is drawn, as decorations, and the stretches of
the document changed since they were last checked. Both follow the text
through every transaction, so an edit above a paragraph moves its
underlines with it. An edit takes away the underlines it touches, so a
word being fixed stops being flagged as it is fixed.

The plugin's view does the checking. A pause after typing, it takes the
changed paragraphs, those on the screen first: one already checked as it
now reads is drawn straight from the checker's cache, and the rest are sent
to be checked, a few at a time, and drawn when the answers come back. Each
paragraph is checked on its own, as a string in which a line break is `\n`,
so a lint at offset `i` is at position `start + i`. A paragraph with
suggestions in it is checked as it would read with them taken, so what
they would take out is not in the string, and its offsets are mapped back
(`blockText`). Code blocks are not checked, nor formulas on lines of their
own; one in a sentence is a word to the checker, and a lint that touches it,
or inline code, is not drawn.

Only what is near the screen is checked: Harper takes about a quarter of a
millisecond a word, so a novel in one document would keep a core busy for
half a minute. The rest waits until the writer scrolls to it.

A misspelling at the caret isn't drawn while the writer is typing: the
word may not be finished. Moving the caret shows it.

## editor/state

The editor's state layer: how a document becomes an
`EditorState`, what the keys and the typed shortcuts do, and the two
transactions an outside writer can ask for.

`EditorState` is the open document — doc, selection, undo history, and
plugin state as one immutable value — and every change to it is a
transaction. Nothing here needs a view, which is why it is tested without
one; `Editor.vue` puts an `EditorView` in front of the state, and
`useEditor` holds the state and dispatches to it.

The keys follow the previous editor's where it had them — Mod-B, Mod-I,
Mod-Shift-S, Mod-Alt-1 through 6, Mod-Shift-7 and 8, Mod-Shift-B, Mod-Alt-C
— Notion's for a formula, Mod-Shift-E, and the reference's for lists: Enter
splits an item, Tab and Shift-Tab nest and lift. In a table they move
between cells and rows (see `editor/tables`). A list's keys and the quote's
take it off again, as their items under a selection do (see
`editor/format`). The typed shortcuts are markdown's own: `# `, `- `,
`1. `, `> `, ` ``` `, `---`, `**bold**` and `$x^2$` as you type
(`$$` for a formula of its own, see `editor/formulas`), and a table's
header row followed by Enter. Quotes, dashes and ellipses are made as they
are typed, as a word processor makes them.

only the one.

## editor/streaming

Text the model is still writing into a call that adds to the
end of a document, shown at the end of it as it arrives.

Shown, not written. Until the call runs the document is as it was: the
text is drawn after the last block by a widget, so none of it is saved,
synced, kept in a version, counted, checked for spelling or undone, and
what the writer types goes in above it. When the call runs, the tool's
append puts the same blocks there and the preview comes off in the same
task, so nothing on the page moves. A call stopped, refused or failed takes
its preview with it, since nothing was written.

Which previews a document shows is this plugin's state, changed by a
transaction as one starts and ends. The text goes around the state, since
it changes a token at a time: `setPreviewText` hands it to the widgets
showing it, which redraw now and then, and only from the first block that
changed.

## editor/suggestions

A suggested change: the words it would take out and those it
would put in, both in the text until the writer accepts or rejects it.

In the editor the two halves are marks, `deletion` and `insertion`, each
with the suggestion's id; in the markdown they are CriticMarkup holding
the id, as a comment's passage is:

    We had a {--cold--}{>>s4k2m1<<}{++narrow++}{>>s4k2m1<<} attic.

What was said about it is a thread on the document's row, by that id, as
a comment's is (see `comments.js`).

A change is laid out block by block, then word by word inside the blocks
it changed, so its marks stay inside blocks: a block whose words are all
one suggestion's insertion is a block it puts in, and one whose words are
all its deletion a block it takes out. A paragraph parted in two is the
paragraph's end taken out and a new paragraph put in; two joined, the
second's words put in at the end of the first and the second taken out.
No mark ever stands for a break between blocks, so accepting and
rejecting always mean one thing.

A block with no words to mark carries the mark itself, put in or taken
out whole: a code block, a rule, a table, an empty block. So does one
changed where words cannot be marked: a code block's text, or a table's
rows or columns. In the markdown its halves stand on lines of their own
around it:

    {--
    ---
    --}{>>s4k2m1<<}

Each change in what is suggested is a suggestion of its own, accepted or
rejected alone: a word cut, a phrase replaced, a sentence rewritten.

A change to a document with suggestions pending is made to the text as it
stands, their insertions out, and they are put back into it after. The
model's own pending suggestions it sees accepted, as Docs shows a writer
theirs: its change is made over them, laid out with them again from the
text as it stands, and goes into one it touches.

Laid out the same way under one id, a change is also how a version of a
document is shown against its text now (`layOut`, and `comparison.js`).

Design: `.llm/suggestions_design.md`.

## suggestChange

A document with a change to it suggested: `before` with what `after` takes
out marked as suggested deletions, and what it puts in as insertions. Null
only when the change cannot be laid out at all.

Each change in it is a suggestion of its own, to be accepted or rejected
alone: the words changed together, with those a word or two apart in a
sentence, and a paragraph parted or joined, or a block put in for one taken
out. The first is `id`, the rest `fresh` ones.

`after` is the text as the model saw it, changed: `before` with the
pending suggestions of others rejected, which is what every reader but the
editor sees, and those of the model's own, `own`, accepted. The change is
laid out from the text as it stands, all of them rejected, so the model's
own are laid out again with it. Where a change touches one of the model's
own, it goes into that one, and where it touches two it joins them under
the older. One of them the change takes back is gone. Then the others'
insertions are put back where they were. Blocks `before` kept are its own,
comments, suggestions and all.

### Parameters

- `before` **[Node][1064]**&#x20;
- `after` **[Node][1064]**&#x20;
- `id` **[string][1055]**&#x20;
- `own` **[Array][1057]<[string][1055]>?** The model's own pending suggestions, oldest first (optional, default `[]`)
- `fresh` (optional, default `newSuggestionId`)

Returns **([Suggested][647] | null)**&#x20;

## layOut

Two documents laid out as one, as a change from the first to the second
is, but under the one id, and with nothing of either side settled first:
`before` with what `after` takes out marked as deletions, and what it puts
in as insertions. The blocks and words both have are as `before` has them,
its comments and pending suggestions with them, and what it alone has
that a pending suggestion is on stays that suggestion's. Null when the
change cannot be laid out. For comparing two texts, which nothing writes
back.

### Parameters

- `before` **[Node][1064]**&#x20;
- `after` **[Node][1064]**&#x20;
- `id` **[string][1055]**&#x20;

Returns **([Node][1064] | null)**&#x20;

model's own in the text as it stands, sharing a place with it, is that
one's, and one touching two joins them under the older. The rest are the
change's, each change a suggestion of its own: parts are one where they
are near (`near`), or where a block put in or taken out whole moves the
words of the change beside it (`moved`). The first keeps `id`, and the
rest are given `fresh` ones. Two of the model's own stay apart however
near they are, unless what the change does between them joins them.

### Parameters

- `laid` **[Node][1064]**&#x20;
- `standing` **[Node][1064]** The text as it stands, which `laid` is laid over
- `id` **[string][1055]**&#x20;
- `own` **[Array][1057]<[string][1055]>** Oldest first
- `places` **[Array][1057]<[Array][1057]<{from: [number][1060], to: [number][1060]}>>** Each of `own`'s, in `standing`
- `fresh` &#x20;

Returns **{doc: [Node][1064], ids: [Array][1057]<[string][1055]>, all: [Array][1057]<[string][1055]>, into: Record<[string][1055], [string][1055]>}**&#x20;

## utils/diff

The shortest edit from one sequence to another, as steps:
what each keeps, what the first loses, what the second adds.

Myers' algorithm, which costs time in the sequences' length times the
size of the edit, and room in the square of the edit's size: cheap for a
few changes in a long text, and given up on past a limit for a rewrite,
which the caller handles as one change. What both share at the ends is
set aside first, the end before the start, so that a sequence's last item
is kept wherever it can be: a Google Doc's last newline cannot be
deleted. Within a change, what goes comes before what comes in. Asked
to, the start is set aside first instead, which lines an addition up
after what it repeats rather than before.

`diff3` lays two versions of a sequence against the one both came from:
the stretches all three share, and between them those where one side or
both changed, for a three-way merge.

`pairUp` pairs two sequences whose items are alike rather than equal, a
table's rows or columns: as many pairs as can be, in order, the likest.

## Step

Type: ({op: `"equal"`, a: [number][1060], b: [number][1060]} | {op: `"delete"`, a: [number][1060]} | {op: `"insert"`, b: [number][1060]})

## diffSequences

The steps from `a` to `b`, items compared with `===`.

### Parameters

- `a` &#x20;
- `b` &#x20;
- `$2` **[Object][1056]** (optional, default `{}`)
  - `$2.maxEdits` (optional, default `Infinity`)
  - `$2.startFirst` (optional, default `false`)

- `options` **[Object][1056]?**&#x20;
  - `options.maxEdits` **[number][1060]?** Past this many deletions and
    insertions, give up
  - `options.startFirst` **[boolean][1061]?** Set aside what the two share at
    the start before what they share at the end

Returns **([Array][1057]<[Step][994]> | null)** Null when the edit is over `maxEdits`

## editor/suggestionText

Suggestions in markdown, for what holds a document's text
rather than its editor state: whether a text has any, the text as one
reader sees it, and text from outside with any markup of theirs read as
meant.

The markup is CriticMarkup holding an id (see `suggestions.js`), and only
the parser tells a half that pairs from one that is text, so a text with
suggestions is read as a document and written out again. A text without
any comes back as it was, untouched.

Every reader but the editor reads the text as it stands: the word count,
explore's digests, a document exported, and the model's reads, its own
suggestions made in its chat. Narration and the spelling checker read the
editor's document and leave the marks out there (`tts/script.js`,
`editor/spelling.js`).

## CLOSE

The close of either half, which a text with a suggestion has.

## INSERTED

A half put in, with what it puts in.

## DELETED

A half taken out.

## holdsSuggestions

Whether a text may hold a suggestion: it has a half's close.

### Parameters

- `content` **([string][1055] | null | [undefined][1062])**&#x20;

Returns **[boolean][1061]**&#x20;

## seenMarkdown

Markdown as one reader sees it: the suggestions `accepted` names accepted,
every other rejected, and comments' markup kept. With none named, the text
as it stands, which is what every reader but the editor reads.

### Parameters

- `content` **[string][1055]**&#x20;
- `accepted` **[Array][1057]<[string][1055]>?** (optional, default `[]`)

Returns **[string][1055]**&#x20;

## textAsItStands

Markdown as a reader of the text reads it, a word count or a digest: as
it stands, each suggestion rejected, and without comments' markup.

### Parameters

- `content` **[string][1055]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][1055]**&#x20;

## withoutSuggestionMarkup

Text from outside with suggestions' markup read as meant: what a half

means the change it marks, and what it writes is never a suggestion of
its own: the tools make those.

### Parameters

- `text` **[string][1055]**&#x20;

Returns **[string][1055]**&#x20;

## editor/tables

Tables in the editor: making one by typing its header row,
moving through it from the keyboard, and the row and column commands its
menu offers.

A table is made the way the rest of the document is, by typing its
markdown: `| Name | Age |` and Enter becomes a table with that header and an
empty row under it; or from the editor's menu (`editor/insert`). Inside one,
Tab and Shift-Tab go from cell to cell, stopping at the first and the last.
Enter goes down a row, and from the last row leaves the table for a
paragraph after it, as Shift-Enter and Mod-Enter do from any cell, and as
they leave a code block. No key adds a row or a column: the editor's menu
does, with `insertRow` and `insertColumn`, which put the caret in what they
add. Backspace on the whole table empties its cells, and on an empty one
deletes it. Rows, columns, and the table itself are taken away from the
menu with `prosemirror-tables`' own commands, and a column is aligned with
`alignColumn`.

The rest is `prosemirror-tables` too: selecting cells, pasting cells, and
keeping every row as wide as the others. Anything else pasted into a cell
is made to fit its one line (`cellPaste`).

## intoCell

Put the caret at the end of the cell that starts at `pos`.

### Parameters

- `tr` **Transaction**&#x20;
- `pos` **[number][1060]** Directly before the cell

Returns **Transaction**&#x20;

## paragraphAfter

A new paragraph after a table, with the caret in it.

### Parameters

- `tr` **Transaction**&#x20;
- `after` **[number][1060]** Directly after the table

Returns **Transaction**&#x20;

## cellsOfRow

The cells a typed header row names: what lies between its pipes, trimmed,
with its marks. Null when the line is not a row — not all text, or not
opened and closed with a pipe.

### Parameters

- `line` **[Node][1064]** A paragraph

Returns **([Array][1057]\<Fragment> | null)**&#x20;

## tableFromRow

Enter at the end of a typed header row, `| Name | Age |`: the row becomes a
table, with an empty row under it and the caret there.

Type: Command

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;
- `dispatch` &#x20;

## nextRow

Enter in a table: down a row, keeping the column. From the last row it
leaves the table for a paragraph after it.

Type: Command

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;
- `dispatch` &#x20;

## insertRow

A row added above or below the caret's, with the caret in it, in the same
column.

### Parameters

- `side` **(`"above"` | `"below"`)**&#x20;

Returns **Command**&#x20;

## insertColumn

A column added left or right of the caret's, with the caret in it, in the
same row.

### Parameters

- `side` **(`"left"` | `"right"`)**&#x20;

Returns **Command**&#x20;

## exitTable

Leave the table for a new paragraph after it.

Type: Command

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;
- `dispatch` &#x20;

## deleteEmptyTable

Backspace or Delete on a whole table whose cells are empty: the table goes,
and the caret goes to the start of what followed it, or the end of what came
before. A table that was all its parent held leaves an empty paragraph,
since the parent has to hold something. With words still in the cells,
`prosemirror-tables` empties them first, so a table goes in two presses, or
three from the start of the paragraph after it, where the first selects it.

Type: Command

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;
- `dispatch` &#x20;

## nextCell

Tab in a table: the next cell, and nowhere from the last, so that the key
does not take the caret out of the editor.

Type: Command

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;
- `dispatch` &#x20;

## previousCell

Shift-Tab in a table: the cell before, and nowhere from the first, so that
the key does not take the caret out of the editor.

Type: Command

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;
- `dispatch` &#x20;

## alignColumn

Align the columns the selection is in, or take their alignment away.

### Parameters

- `align` **(`"left"` | `"center"` | `"right"` | null)**&#x20;

Returns **Command**&#x20;

## alignmentAt

The column alignment the selection is in, as the first row has it.

### Parameters

- `state` &#x20;

Returns **([string][1055] | null)**&#x20;

## cellPaste

Pasting into a cell. Cells copied from a table are `prosemirror-tables`'s,
pasted over the cells from this one on. Anything else goes into the one
line this cell has: a line of text as it is, and more than that as its
words, a space where each line or block ended. Left to the usual paste,
each line would be made a cell of its own, since a cell is the only
textblock a row can hold, and laid over the cells beside this one.

Ahead of `tableEditing`, which would paste those cells.

Returns **Plugin**&#x20;
